name: GitHub
use_case: read and act on a user's repositories, issues and pull requests

verdict.label: Self-serve · minutes
verdict.summary: No approval step: you can register an OAuth app and connect real users in about 15 minutes. The real launch risk is your users' organizations, which block OAuth apps by default until an org owner approves yours.
verdict.wait: None from GitHub (org-owner approvals happen on your customers' side)
verdict.gating_step: Customer organizations restrict OAuth apps by default; each org owner must approve your app

concept: GitHub has two kinds of app. An OAuth app is authorized by an individual user and acts as that user, limited by scopes. A GitHub App is installed on an account or org, picks specific repositories, and uses fine-grained permissions. For a Composio custom auth config, you register one OAuth app, and every user who connects authorizes that same client ID.

paths.name: OAuth app (this guide)
paths.when: You want users to connect their own GitHub identity quickly. Simplest path; what most agent integrations use.

paths.name: GitHub App
paths.when: Customers want repo-by-repo control, higher rate limits that scale with installs, or your agent must act as a bot, not as a person. GitHub itself recommends GitHub Apps for new projects.

composio.managed_note: Composio's GitHub toolkit lists a Composio-managed OAuth app (OAuth2), so you can build today without registering anything.
when_own_app: Production: users should see your app name on the consent screen, not “Composio”.
You need scopes beyond Composio's defaults.
You need your own rate-limit quota (managed apps share quota across Composio users).
You need faster polling triggers than the managed 15-minute minimum.
Self-hosted or regional instances of the provider.

stages.name: Build & test (works today)
stages.summary: Everything here is self-serve. In our test, the app was created and showed a Client ID immediately, with no review and no waiting.

limits.text: A user or organization can own up to 100 OAuth apps.
Tested: registration to Client ID took about 3 minutes, and the app was usable at once (“0 users”, no pending state).

steps.title: Decide who owns the app
steps.detail: Register it under your company's GitHub organization, not a personal account, so it survives people leaving. You need admin rights on that org.

steps.title: Open Settings → Developer settings → OAuth Apps → New OAuth App
steps.detail: If you've never created one, the button says “Register a new application”. The form page is titled “Register a new OAuth app”.

steps.title: Fill in name, homepage URL and description
steps.detail: Users see these on the authorization screen. GitHub warns to use only information you consider public, with no internal URLs.

steps.title: Add the redirect URI
steps.detail: The form now calls this section “Redirect URIs”, not “Authorization callback URL” as GitHub's docs still say. Paste Composio's callback URL into the Redirect URI box. “Add redirect URI” allows up to 10 per app. Leave the per-URI “Allow wildcard matching” box unticked.

steps.title: Keep “Expire user access tokens” on
steps.detail: It's ticked by default on the registration form. Tokens last 8 hours and come with a 6-month refresh token. Composio stores and refreshes tokens for you. After registration the box no longer appears on the General page; it lives with the app's other settings (likely “Optional features”).

steps.title: Generate a client secret and create the Composio auth config
steps.detail: Copy the Client ID and secret into Composio (Create Auth Config → GitHub → OAuth2 → use your own developer credentials). Never commit the secret.

steps.title: Connect your own GitHub account end to end
steps.detail: Run one connection through your app and call a read-only tool to confirm the token and scopes work.

stages.name: Go to production
stages.summary: GitHub doesn't review OAuth apps. Production readiness is about scopes, your customers' org policies, and token handling.

limits.text: OAuth apps are rate-limited to 2,000 access-token requests per hour. Exceeding it temporarily blocks new tokens.

steps.title: Request the narrowest scopes
steps.detail: OAuth app access is limited only by scopes. A token can reach every repository the user can. Ask only for what your agent's tools need.

steps.title: Tell customers to approve your app in their GitHub org
steps.detail: New organizations have OAuth app access restrictions enabled by default. Members can't grant your app access to org repos; they can only request that an owner approve it. Put this in your onboarding docs.

steps.title: Optional: list on GitHub Marketplace
steps.detail: Only needed for discovery or billing through GitHub. It isn't required for users to authorize your app.

requirements.item: GitHub account or org admin rights
requirements.detail: To register the app under an organization.
Shown to users on the authorization screen.
Tokens now expire after 8 hours by default. Composio handles refresh; custom code must too.

gotchas.title: Customer orgs block your app by default
gotchas.detail: A user can authorize your app and still see none of their company's private repos until an org owner approves it. This is the most common “it connected but sees nothing” report.

gotchas.title: Tokens expire now (changed August 2026)
gotchas.detail: Many guides and libraries still say GitHub OAuth tokens never expire and that OAuth apps support only one callback URL. Both changed in August 2026: new apps get 8-hour tokens plus refresh tokens, and up to 10 redirect URIs.

gotchas.title: A new app means everyone re-authorizes
gotchas.detail: Tokens are bound to the client ID. Edit the existing app to add callbacks or rotate the secret; don't create a new one.

gotchas.title: All-or-nothing repo access
gotchas.detail: OAuth apps can't be limited to selected repositories. Security-conscious customers may ask for a GitHub App instead.

blockers.cause: The redirect_uri sent doesn't exactly match a registered callback URL.
blockers.fix: Register Composio's callback URL exactly (scheme, host, path), or omit redirect_uri so GitHub uses the registered default.

blockers.symptom: Connected, but the agent can't see org repositories
blockers.cause: The org has OAuth app access restrictions on (the default for new orgs).
blockers.fix: Have the user request approval; an org owner approves it under Organization settings → Third-party access.

blockers.cause: GitHub suspended the app, typically for reported abuse, spam or API misuse.

agent: Pick the minimum scopes from your tool list
Draft the app name, description and homepage copy
Write customer-facing “approve our app in your org” instructions
Run a test connection and verify scopes with a read-only call
you: Sign in and register the app (requires org admin)
Generate and store the client secret
Ask pilot customers' org owners to approve the app

uncertainties: Composio's FAQ asks whether GitHub Apps are supported; we didn't verify how a GitHub App's user-to-server flow behaves inside a Composio auth config.
